guides.title: From First Contact to the Founding
guides.summary: The century between Earth's first warp flight and the Federation charter, and why the setting treats it as the hinge.

sections.heading: The Flight and the Meeting
sections.body: The setting dates the beginning of everything to a single, deliberately unglamorous event: a first crewed faster-than-light flight, made from a damaged and impoverished post-war Earth, in a vessel converted from a weapon. The flight is detected by a passing Vulcan survey ship, which lands and makes contact. The framing matters. Earth is not discovered because it is admirable; it is discovered because it crossed a technical threshold, and the threshold is the same one the Prime Directive later codifies. The civilisation that arrives does not rescue Earth or govern it. It introduces itself and then, to Earth's considerable frustration, spends decades declining to hand over very much. What follows is presented as a recovery rather than a transformation: roughly a century in which Earth rebuilds, ends its wars and its poverty, and turns outward. The setting is consistent that this was work, that it was contested, and that contact was the occasion for it rather than the cause.

sections.heading: The Difficult Apprenticeship
sections.body: The decades between contact and the founding are drawn as an awkward mentorship. Vulcans, with far greater capability and a much longer memory of what contact does to young civilisations, act as a restraint — convinced that humans were expanding faster than their judgement could support, and not always wrong. Humans experienced this as condescension, and were not always wrong either. The period also contains Earth's first sustained encounters with powers that were not interested in mentorship: early, costly contacts with the civilisations that would become its principal rivals, and at least one war fought without either side seeing the other's face. The result is a founding generation shaped by having been both patronised and attacked, which is a reasonable explanation for an institution as insistent on procedure, consent and the rights of small powers as the Federation turns out to be.

sections.heading: The Charter
sections.body: The union is founded by four powers that were, on any reasonable assessment, poorly suited to each other: humans, Vulcans, Andorians and Tellarites. Vulcans distrusted human impulsiveness. Andorians and Vulcans had a long history of confrontation. Tellarites regard argument itself as a form of courtesy and were regarded by everyone else as impossible. That the charter was signed by exactly those four is the setting's central political claim, and it is made deliberately: the union works not because its members are alike but because they agreed on a procedure for disagreeing. A federation of the naturally compatible would prove nothing. The charter reserves defence, exploration and external diplomacy to the union and leaves everything else to the members; it guarantees a set of individual rights no member may abridge; and it makes membership voluntary in both directions. Those provisions are what every later crisis tests.

sections.heading: Why the Period Is Told and Retold
sections.body: This century is returned to more often than any other, and usually when the setting wants to remind itself what the institution was for. It contains the founding's least flattering material — the mistakes, the paternalism, the wars fought blind — which is precisely why it works as a corrective to the later eras' confidence. It also establishes the pattern the whole setting runs on. A capable civilisation meets a less capable one and has to decide what it owes it. A union is offered to people who have excellent reasons to refuse. A principle is written down before anyone knows what it will cost. Every subsequent century is a variation on those three.

guides.title: The Dominion War
guides.summary: The conflict that tested whether the Federation's principles were commitments or comforts.

sections.heading: The Adversary
sections.body: The Dominion is a power from a distant region of the galaxy, organised on a rigid three-tier structure: a small ruling caste of shapeshifters, a genetically engineered client species bred to administer and negotiate, and a soldier species bred for war and biochemically dependent on a drug only their masters supply. It is not an empire that conquered its subjects so much as one that manufactured them. This makes it a genuinely different opponent from the setting's usual rivals. There is no Dominion public to appeal to, no internal opposition to encourage, and no possibility of the soldiers defecting while their supply is controlled. Its rulers regard other forms of life as inherently chaotic and their own dominion as an act of order rather than of greed, which is a far harder position to argue against than simple ambition. Its shapeshifting rulers also make it a war of paranoia before it is a war of fleets. An enemy able to replace any individual undetectably attacks trust itself, and much of the run-up to open conflict consists of allied powers becoming dangerous to each other.

sections.heading: How It Started
sections.body: Contact came through a stable passage connecting Federation space to the Dominion's region, which turned a remote frontier posting into the most strategically important object in known space overnight. The Dominion's early moves were characteristic: not invasion, but infiltration, destabilisation and the encouragement of existing enmities among the powers on the other side. The Federation's response was slow and internally contested, which the setting depicts honestly rather than flatteringly. Intelligence services expanded their reach, civil liberties came under pressure, an attempted military intervention in Federation government was narrowly averted, and a great deal of what was done in the name of security would not have survived being said out loud. Open war followed the Dominion's alliance with a neighbouring power and its seizure of the passage. The Federation entered it allied with the Klingon Empire, and later, after considerable manoeuvring, with the Romulans — an alliance of three powers who had spent most of their history preparing to fight each other.

sections.heading: What the War Did to the Federation
sections.body: The war is the setting's most sustained examination of what its own protagonists will do under genuine pressure, and the answers are not comfortable. Losses ran to the millions. Whole sectors changed hands. The fleet built warships rather than explorers, and an institution that had spent a century insisting it was not a military found itself conducting one of the largest wars in the region's history. The specific compromises are the point. A covert service acted without oversight and, on at least one occasion, in ways the Federation's own charter plainly forbids. Officers deceived allies into the war on the reasoning that the alternative was defeat. A biological weapon was employed against the enemy's ruling caste. Each of these is presented with the argument for it fully made and then not excused. This is why the war matters to the setting beyond its scale. A utopia that has never been tested is an assertion; one that has been tested, has partly failed, and has to live with the record is an argument.

sections.heading: Afterwards
sections.body: The war ended with the Dominion's withdrawal, negotiated rather than annihilated, and with the region's powers exhausted. Cardassia, having allied with the Dominion and then turned against it, was devastated on a scale the setting refuses to soften. The Klingon Empire and the Federation emerged as genuine allies rather than nominal ones. The Romulans returned to their own concerns. For the Federation the aftermath is a rebuilding both material and institutional. Fleets are replaced faster than trust is, and the setting's subsequent material is populated by officers who fought and by an organisation quietly reckoning with what it authorised. The war also settled an argument that had run through the setting for decades: whether the Federation's values could survive contact with an enemy that did not share them. The answer given is a qualified yes — they survived, damaged, and only because enough individuals insisted on them at moments when insisting was expensive.

guides.title: The Khitomer Accords
guides.summary: How a century of hostility with the Klingon Empire ended, and what it cost the people who ended it.

sections.heading: The Situation
sections.body: The Federation and the Klingon Empire spent generations in a hostility that neither could win and neither could end: a long armed peace punctuated by open fighting, a neutral zone between them, and two societies that had built a great deal of themselves around regarding the other as the enemy. What broke the stalemate was a catastrophe rather than a change of heart. A disaster in Klingon space — the setting places it at a moon whose destruction crippled the Empire's energy production — left the Empire facing decades of decline and unable to sustain the confrontation. Its leadership concluded, over furious internal opposition, that peace was now the only survivable option. The Federation's position was not straightforwardly generous either. Some in its leadership saw an opportunity to accept a rival's collapse rather than to prevent it, and the argument about whether to help was genuine.

sections.heading: The Conspiracy
sections.body: The negotiations were nearly destroyed by a conspiracy drawing on both sides at once — Federation officers, Klingon officers and a third party, cooperating to assassinate the peacemakers and ensure the war continued. That detail is the most durable thing about the episode and the setting knows it. The reasoning attributed to the plotters is not stupidity. Careers, industries, doctrines and identities had been built on the confrontation, and on both sides there were people who genuinely believed their civilisation would be worse without an enemy. A soldier who has spent forty years preparing for a war does not welcome being told it is over. It is also the setting's clearest statement that peace is made by people who have to overcome their own side. The officers who saved the talks did so against colleagues, and several of them had spent their careers as enthusiastic participants in the hostility they were now ending.

sections.heading: What Was Signed
sections.body: The Accords established peace, opened the border, and set the framework that eventually became a full alliance. The neutral zone was dissolved over time. Exchange programmes followed, and within a few generations a Klingon officer serving aboard a Federation starship had become unremarkable — which, to anyone present at the signing, would have been unimaginable. The agreement was not a merger and the setting is careful about that. The Empire remained the Empire, with its own politics, its own honour system and its own view of the Federation as slightly ridiculous. Alliance did not mean agreement, and the relationship was broken and remade more than once afterwards. Its most severe test came during the Dominion War, when the alliance held and both powers fought a war neither could have survived alone. That is the retrospective vindication the setting offers for the whole business.

sections.heading: Why It Is the Setting's Favourite Story
sections.body: The Accords are the setting's argument about how enmity ends, and the argument has three parts. It ends because circumstances force it, not because anyone became better. It is opposed most fiercely by the people who understand it best. And it is completed by individuals who have to act against their own instincts, in public, at personal cost. The setting also uses it to say something uncomfortable about its own protagonists. The officers who made the peace were not free of prejudice; several had lost family, and their objections to the Klingons were sincere and, by their own lights, earned. They did it anyway, which the setting treats as the harder and more admirable version. It is why the Klingon relationship is the setting's deepest. An enemy who becomes an ally without becoming similar is a far more interesting arrangement than either war or agreement, and everything the setting later does with Klingon characters rests on this.

guides.title: The Earth-Romulan War
guides.summary: The conflict that made the Federation necessary, fought between powers that never saw each other.

sections.heading: Before the Founding
sections.body: The war predates the Federation and is the reason it exists. Earth, barely a century into interstellar travel, fought the Romulan Star Empire in a conflict that reached Earth's own system and was won only with the help of the same neighbouring powers that would shortly afterwards become co-founders of a permanent union. The setting places it in the era before the alliance was formalised, when Vulcans, Andorians, Tellarites and humans were cooperating warily and without any structure obliging them to. The war supplied the argument that structure was needed: four powers who nearly lost separately concluded they would not survive the next one that way. Its scale is described as enormous for the period and its cost as formative. A generation of humans grew up understanding that the galaxy contained things that would come for them, which is a significant part of why the Federation was built the way it was.

sections.heading: A War Without a Face
sections.body: The war's most distinctive feature is that neither side saw the other. Fought with primitive sensors, at ranges and in eras before visual communication was routine, it was conducted entirely through instruments — and it ended without either party having laid eyes on their enemy. That detail is one of the setting's best and it pays off much later. When a Federation vessel finally encounters a Romulan face on a viewscreen, generations after the armistice, the revelation that they resemble Vulcans lands on a bridge crew including a Vulcan officer, in front of colleagues who now have to decide what they think. The absence of a face also shaped the peace. An enemy nobody has seen is easy to imagine and hard to negotiate with, and the long paranoid silence that followed the armistice was possible precisely because neither side had any concrete idea what the other was.

sections.heading: How It Ended
sections.body: It ended not in victory but in an armistice negotiated remotely, establishing a neutral zone that neither side might enter on pain of war. No delegation met. The terms were agreed through intermediaries and instruments, and the border was drawn on a chart by people who had never been introduced. The zone held for generations, which is a remarkable outcome for an agreement made under those conditions, and it held because both sides were exhausted rather than because anything was resolved. The grievances that started the war were left entirely in place, which is why the eventual re-emergence of the Romulans is treated as a resumption rather than a new crisis. The outposts along that line, watching an empty band of space for decades, are the setting's image of the whole arrangement: enormous vigilance directed at a silence.

sections.heading: What It Established
sections.body: Three things date from this war and outlast it. The Federation itself, founded in its aftermath by powers who had learned what fighting alone cost. The Neutral Zone, which shapes the setting's map for centuries. And the Federation's treaty renunciation of certain capabilities, which is bound up in the same settlement. It also fixed the Romulans as the setting's oldest antagonist and the one it understands least, which is by design. An enemy encountered at the very beginning, fought without contact, and then not seen again for generations is a much stranger presence than one negotiated with continuously. For the Federation's own self-image, the war is the founding proof. An organisation that exists because its members nearly died separately has a different character from one founded on shared enthusiasm, and the Federation's stubbornness about collective security makes more sense read against it.
